description: Inventory is cash converted into a guess about the future, and store work is far more skilled than outsiders assume. Avoid retail-apocalypse framing entirely.

questions.text: You are converting cash into a bet on what people will want months from now. How do you make that call?
questions.lands_because: Frames buying as the forecasting problem it actually is. Buyers rarely get treated as the risk-takers they are and respond well to it.
followups: What did you get badly wrong, and what did you learn from it?

questions.text: What happens to the inventory that does not sell?
questions.lands_because: Markdowns, liquidation, returns processing, and destruction are the industry's least examined and most consequential machinery.
followups: How much of your margin does that quietly eat?

questions.text: What does a great store manager do that would not show up in any report?
questions.lands_because: Treats store operations as skilled work - scheduling, training, de-escalation, floor sense - which the industry's own corporate side often fails to do.
followups: Does the company know who those people are?

questions.text: What did you learn about your customers from returns that you never learned from sales?
questions.lands_because: Returns are a rich and under-discussed data source, and the operational cost of them is a story in itself.
followups: What have you changed because of it?

questions.text: What does the platform you sell on take from you, and what do you get for it?
questions.lands_because: Marketplace and ad-spend dependency is the defining economic condition for most sellers, and the honest accounting is rarely offered publicly.
followups: What happens to your business if those terms change?

questions.text: What have you watched customer behavior do in the last few years that surprised you?
questions.lands_because: Frontline retail is a genuine sensor for economic and social change, and operators notice patterns long before they appear in the data.
followups: Do you think that is permanent?
